questions.knowledge_point: Computing Limits of Piecewise Functions with a Gap in the Domain
questions.problem:
Find ${lim}_{x\to 1}f(x)$ for the function given by

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}(x-1)^{3}-2\, & \text{ for }\,x\le -1 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡x+2\, & \text{ for }\,1\le x\le 10.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
To compute ${lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x),$ we must compute the left and right-sided limits separately.

However, the left-sided limit ${lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{-}}f(x)$ does not exist since $f(x)$ is not defined on the interval $x\in (-1,1).$ 

Consequently, the overall limit does not exist either:

$$
{lim}_{x\to 1}f(x)=\text{DNE}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the One-Sided Limits of a Piecewise Function when the Limits Do Not Coincide
questions.worked_solution:
Approaching from the left, we have $x<2,$ so we use the expression $g(x)={x}^{2}+x-2.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}g(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}({x}^{2}+x-2) \\  & ={2}^{2}+2-2 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Approaching from the right, we have $x\ge 2,$ so we use the expression $g(x)=\frac{3-\sqrt{x+7}}{{x}^{2}-1}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}g(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}\frac{3-\sqrt{x+7}}{{x}^{2}-1} \\  & =\frac{3-\sqrt{2+7}}{{2}^{2}-1} \\  & =\frac{3-\sqrt{9}}{4-1} \\  & =\frac{3-3}{3} \\  & =\frac{0}{3} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}g(x)=4,\,{lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}g(x)=0.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the One-Sided Limits of a Piecewise Function when the Limits Do Not Coincide
questions.worked_solution:
Approaching from the left, we have $x<\pi ,$ so we use the expression $f(x)=x+\pi .$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {\pi }^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {\pi }^{-}}(x+\pi ) \\  & =\pi +\pi  \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing Limits of Piecewise Functions with a Gap in the Domain
questions.worked_solution:
Approaching $x=-2$ from the left, we have $x<-2,$ so we use the expression $f(x)=(x+2)^{3}+7.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-2)^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to (-2)^{-}}[(x+2)^{3}+7] \\  & =(-2+2)^{3}+7 \\  & ={0}^{3}+7 \\  & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, approaching $x=4$ from the right, we have $x\ge 4,$ so we use the expression $f(x)=\sqrt{x-4}-1.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {4}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {4}^{+}}(\sqrt{x-4}-1) \\  & =\sqrt{4-4}-1 \\  & =\sqrt{0}-1 \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving for a Constant Such that the Limit of a Piecewise Function Exists
questions.problem:
For the piecewise function 

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}c\, & \text{ for }\,x<2 \\ \frac{1}{3}\, & \text{ for }\,x=2 \\ {x}^{3}-3\, & \text{ for }\,x>2\end{aligned}
$$

it is known that ${lim}_{x\to 2}f(x)$ exists. What is the value of constant $c?$

$c=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
In order for ${lim}_{x\to 2}f(x)$ to exist, the left and right-sided limits must both exist and be equal.

- Approaching from the left, we have $x<2,$ so we use the expression $f(x)=c.$ We get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}c \\  & =c\,.\end{aligned}
$$

- Approaching from the right, we have $x>2,$ so we use the expression $f(x)={x}^{3}-3.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}{x}^{3}-3 \\  & ={(2)}^{3}-3 \\  & =8-3 \\  & =5\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the left and right-sided limits must be equal, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}f(x) \\ c & =5.\end{aligned}
$$
